domains.title: Jowangshin, the Kitchen King Spirit
domains.subtitle: guardian of the hearth, food, and household fortune
domains.lead: Jowangshin is the kitchen king spirit who protects the hearth, supervises the preparation of food, and reports on the household to heaven in Korean tradition. The name means "Kitchen king spirit" and belongs to the domain "Kitchen, Hearth." Jowangshin is the spirit of the kitchen hearth, one of the most important household deities in Korean folk religion. The figure is believed to record the affairs of the household and report them to heaven, so housewives observed taboos such as not cursing in the kitchen and keeping the hearth clean.

cards.name: Kitchen King Spirit

mythology.lead: The mythology of Jowangshin is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Munjeon Bonpuri
myths.text: In the Jeju epic Munjeon Bonpuri, the heroine Yeosan Buin suffers unjust death and is revived by her sons. She is appointed by Cheonjiwang as Jowangshin, the hearth goddess who dwells in every kitchen and reports on family conduct.

myths.title: The Five Taboos
myths.text: Traditional households observed five rules in the kitchen: do not curse, do not sit on the hearth, do not place feet on the hearth, keep the kitchen clean, and avoid disrespect to the fire. Breaking these rules risked misfortune.

myths.title: Sending the Report to Heaven
myths.text: At the end of the lunar year families performed a rite to send Jowangshin to heaven with a favourable report. Sticky foods such as malt taffy were offered in the hope that the spirit's lips would be sealed by sweetness.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 竈 (jo, "kitchen, hearth"), 王 (wang, "king"), and 神 (sin, "spirit, deity"). Read 조왕신 in Korean, it denotes the sovereign spirit of the domestic hearth.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Jowangshin, the Hangul form is 조왕신 and the Hanja form is 竈王神. Hangul ‘조왕신’ and Hanja ‘竈王神’; the figure is also written Jowangsin. The ASCII form jowangshin is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Jowangshin is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Jowangshin is closely parallel to the Chinese Zao Jun (Kitchen God), and the two figures probably influenced each other through Sino-Korean cultural exchange. Yet the Korean figure has its own origin epic, the Munjeon Bonpuri, and is embedded in distinct shamanic ritual. Confucian households domesticated the cult by assigning it to women's observance, while Buddhist temples sometimes honoured the hearth spirit as a protector. Today Jowangshin survives in household customs, year-end rituals, and the lingering sense that the kitchen is the moral centre of the home.
lore.culturalLegacy: Jowangshin continues to shape Korean domestic culture. The kitchen remains a symbol of family care and moral order, and traces of the hearth-spirit cult appear in New Year customs, housewarming rituals, and the reverence shown to elders who cook. The Munjeon Bonpuri is performed in Jeju shamanic rituals and has been recognised as part of Korea's intangible cultural heritage. Scholars study Jowangshin as an example of how women's labour is sacralised and how the household becomes a microcosm of cosmic justice.
lore.extendedMeditation: Jowangshin invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
